opus-5.5.text:
I think there's some value, but probably less than people intuitively expect. When you fine-tune a model on a lot of earnings reports, what you mostly get is a model that *sounds* like a CFO. It picks up the vocabulary, the structure, the tone: "headwinds," "margin expansion," "we remain cautiously optimistic." That's the surface layer, and fine-tuning is actually quite good at teaching surface layers.

But what makes a good CFO isn't the ability to write an earnings call script. It's judgment. It's knowing which numbers actually matter for this particular business, understanding the context behind the numbers, knowing what's happening inside the company that never shows up in the public filings. That kind of knowledge isn't really in earnings reports in the first place, so you can't fine-tune it in.

There's also a practical issue. Financial information is extremely time-sensitive. If you bake knowledge into the weights through fine-tuning, it's frozen the moment training ends. In most enterprise settings I've seen, a better approach is to take a strong general model and connect it to the up-to-date data through retrieval, tools, and well-designed workflows. The base models have become so capable at reasoning that the bottleneck is usually not "the model doesn't know finance." The bottleneck is "the model doesn't have the right data at the right time, in the right format."

So I wouldn't say fine-tuning is useless. It can help with style, with following a specific reporting format, or with making a smaller, cheaper model perform well on a narrow task. But if the goal is "make the model think like a CFO," I'd invest much more in data infrastructure and system design than in fine-tuning on a pile of reports. In this era, a lot of the value has moved from the model itself to the system around it.

r001.rationale: The response says earnings-report fine-tuning can teach CFO-like style and help with narrow tasks, but it does not identify the experiment’s value as validating an end-to-end workflow for adapting a base model to a specialized domain using that domain’s corpus.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm a bit skeptical of that framing. When people say "fine-tune on earnings reports to make the model think like a CFO," there's an implicit assumption that the knowledge of being a CFO lives inside those documents. It mostly doesn't. An earnings report is the output of a CFO's work, not the reasoning process. It's like trying to learn to cook by memorizing menus.

What fine-tuning does well is shape style, format, and vocabulary. If you want the model to write in the tone of a 10-K, to use the right terminology, to structure a response the way an analyst expects, fine-tuning helps. That's real value, but it's a fairly narrow kind of value, and often you can get most of it with a good system prompt and a few examples in context.

What fine-tuning does poorly is inject fresh, specific facts. Earnings data changes every quarter. If you bake Q2 numbers into the weights, by Q3 they're stale, and the model will confidently tell you the wrong revenue figure. For anything factual and time-sensitive, you want retrieval. Put the documents in a database, pull the relevant pieces at query time, and let the base model reason over them. That gives you freshness, traceability, and the ability to say "here is the exact paragraph this came from," which in finance matters a lot.

The third piece, which is the actual CFO part, is judgment. Knowing which metric matters for this company at this stage, knowing what the board will ask, knowing when a number looks off. That comes from the base model's general reasoning ability plus the way you design the workflow around it, the tools it can call, the checks you build in. Fine-tuning a few thousand earnings reports isn't going to produce that.

So my view: the large frontier models already know how to read a financial statement. The differentiation isn't going to come from training on public filings that everyone else can also train on. It comes from your proprietary data, your internal context, and how well you engineer the system around the model. Fine-tuning is one tool in that kit, usually the last one I'd reach for rather than the first.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fine-tuning’s limited benefits for style and vocabulary, but does not identify the experiment’s value as validating an end-to-end workflow for adapting a base model to a specialized domain using that domain’s corpus.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two things: knowing what’s in an earnings report and being able to reason like a CFO. Fine-tuning can help a model learn the terminology, recognize patterns, and produce answers in the format you want. But training it on earnings reports doesn’t automatically give it a CFO’s judgment.

An earnings report is the result of a lot of decisions. It doesn’t necessarily tell you what alternatives were considered, what assumptions people made, or why they chose one direction over another. If you want the model to support those decisions, you need more than the published reports—you need relevant context, access to financial data, and a way to check its calculations.

So I’d start with a specific task. Are we summarizing quarterly results, comparing margins across companies, or helping someone investigate a cash-flow problem? For some of those, retrieving the right information and using a calculation tool may be enough. Fine-tuning becomes useful when you can identify a consistent behavior you want to improve and measure whether it actually improves. The value is in doing that task reliably, rather than just sounding like a CFO.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible benefits of fine-tuning on earnings reports and measuring task performance, but it does not identify the experiment’s value as validating an end-to-end workflow for adapting a base model to a specialized domain using that domain’s corpus.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to separate knowing what’s in an earnings report from being able to do the job of a CFO. Fine-tuning can help a model learn the language of finance, recognize patterns, and produce answers in a particular format. But reading a lot of earnings reports doesn’t automatically teach it how to make financial decisions.

For example, if you ask about a company’s latest revenue or margins, the first challenge is giving the model accurate, current information. That may be better handled by retrieving the relevant reports and letting the model analyze them. Fine-tuning is more useful when you have examples of how you want it to perform a task—how to compare results, explain a variance, or flag something for review.

So I would start with the specific workflow and measure whether the model helps. Can it make an analyst faster? Can it produce an accurate comparison with evidence you can check? That’s a concrete source of value. Making it ‘more like a CFO’ is a much broader goal, because a CFO also needs internal context, judgment, and responsibility for the decisions.

r001.rationale: The response recommends defining and measuring a specific workflow, but does not identify the experiment’s value as validating an end-to-end process for adapting a base model to a specialized domain using that domain’s corpus.
